content:
roc fmt, changes this:

expect [1, 2, 3] |> List.keep_if(|_| Bool.False) |> List.is_empty()

to this:

expect [1, 2, 3] |> List.keep_if(|_| Bool.False) |> List.is_empty

it removes the () on List.is_empty, is this intended behaviour? If so it is really confusing, I think the () should stay, so it is clear that it is a function.
Yes, it's intended behaviour, I remember discussions about that. I think it's just a matter of style. I agree that it's a bit inconsistent.

By the way, in your examples I would use static dispatch instead:

[1,2,3].keep_if(|_| Bool.False).is_empty()
also you don't need to write Bool.False unless you really want to; False will work just fine! :smile:

Hmm, okay thanks. For own functions, that e.g. work on Lists your suggestion does not work, and I would love to have the input value on the left and and what is tested on the right, so it is really good readable.

own_keep = |list, fun| list.keep_if(fun)
expect [1, 2, 3] |> own_keep(|_| False) |> List.is_empty

I think this would be the most elegant, but it does not work.

own_keep = |list, fun| list.keep_if(fun)
expect [1, 2, 3] |> own_keep(|_| False).is_empty()
expect [1, 2, 3].own_keep(|_| False).is_empty()

Love the |> pipe operator.
Was just wondering and these are just small things I wanted to explore, thank you :)

You actually need an extra space in this case. This works:

expect [1, 2, 3] |> own_keep(|_| False) .is_empty()

roc fmt will add parentheses to avoid any confusion:

expect ([1, 2, 3] |> own_keep(|_| False)).is_empty()

But you'll often want to define a pipe chain across multiple lines:

expect [1, 2, 3]
    |> own_keep(|_| False)
    .is_empty()

Interesting, this looks nice and lovely:

expect [1, 2, 3] |> own_keep(|_| False) .is_empty()

Unlucky that fmt adds the parentheses.
I'm not sure you can have a space after the dot, I think it must be before only (afk rn)

Just tested it, the compiler is really mad about that space after the dot, it gives it four errors. :sweat_smile: 

── ✗ expected record accessor ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── that-dot.roc:2:41

I was parsing access after `.`, and I expected a field name or tuple index.

expect [1, 2, 3] |> own_keep(|_| False) . is_empty()
                                        ^

Required record access uses .name, optional record access uses .?name, and tuple access uses .0. Accessor names must be lowercase and adjacent to their punctuation.

For example:
    person.name
    maybe_person.?name
    pair.0

I found . here.

── ✗ unexpected statement ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── that-dot.roc:2:43

I was parsing a statement, and this token cannot start a statement here.

expect [1, 2, 3] |> own_keep(|_| False) . is_empty()
                                          ^^^^^^^^

Statements can be declarations, type annotations, imports, expectations, returns, crashes, loops, or expression statements inside a block.

For example:
    answer = 42

I found is_empty here.
Names that start with lowercase letters are value names or record field names, depending on the surrounding syntax.

── ✗ unexpected statement ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── that-dot.roc:2:51

I was parsing a statement, and this token cannot start a statement here.

expect [1, 2, 3] |> own_keep(|_| False) . is_empty()
                                                  ^

Statements can be declarations, type annotations, imports, expectations, returns, crashes, loops, or expression statements inside a block.

For example:
    answer = 42

I found ( here.

── ✗ unexpected statement ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── that-dot.roc:2:52

I was parsing a statement, and this token cannot start a statement here.

expect [1, 2, 3] |> own_keep(|_| False) . is_empty()
                                                   ^

Statements can be declarations, type annotations, imports, expectations, returns, crashes, loops, or expression statements inside a block.

For example:
    answer = 42

I found ) here.
This closes the current construct, so the parser was looking for the missing item before it.
